page.title: Lesson Overview
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 1 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Figurative Language and Mood

Lesson Focus

Primary standard: MLA.CW.POE.02—use and analyze figurative language to create mood.
Supporting standards: MLA.CW.WR.07 (connotation, denotation, style) and MLA.CW.COM.03 (craft reasoning).

What You Will Learn

  • Distinguish literal meaning from figurative meaning.
  • Analyze how comparison, personification, imagery, symbol, sound, and connotation shape mood.
  • Select precise evidence and explain the device → association → reader effect chain.
  • Revise a poem so its details create a consistent but nuanced mood.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 1 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task

Record every core term and its complete meaning in your writer’s notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context.

TermMeaningExample
figurative languageLanguage whose meaning extends beyond the literal words.“The moon watched from the window” communicates more than a literal description.
literal meaningThe direct, dictionary-level meaning.In “the glass broke,” the words describe an actual physical event.
moodThe emotional atmosphere a reader experiences.Dark rooms and uneven footsteps create an uneasy mood.
toneThe speaker’s or writer’s attitude toward the subject.Calling the storm “a welcome interruption” creates an appreciative tone.
simileA comparison using like or as.“The page shook like a trapped wing.”
metaphorA direct comparison stating one thing is another.“Her promise was an anchor.”
personificationGiving human action or qualities to something nonhuman.“The radiator complained all night.”
imageryLanguage appealing to sight, sound, touch, taste, or smell.“Cold rain needled the back of his neck.”
symbolA concrete object or image carrying an additional idea.A repaired bridge may represent renewed trust when the poem supports that meaning.
connotationThe feelings or associations attached to a word.“Home” can suggest safety beyond its dictionary meaning.
denotationA word’s direct dictionary definition.The denotation of “dawn” is the beginning of daylight.
sound deviceA pattern such as repetition, alliteration, consonance, or onomatopoeia that shapes emphasis or mood.Repeated soft s sounds can make a line feel hushed.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each meaning to the correct lesson term. Choose Check, review the correct matches, and retry. This is ungraded practice; no screenshot or extra submission is required.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Choose A or B before opening the feedback.

Which explanation correctly separates mood from tone?

A. Mood is the reader’s experienced atmosphere; tone is the attitude communicated by the speaker’s language.
B. Mood and tone are interchangeable names for any emotion mentioned in a poem.
Check your choice and reasoning

A is correct. Mood describes an atmosphere experienced by the reader, while tone describes an attitude conveyed through language. B incorrectly treats the concepts as identical and ignores the evidence needed to support either interpretation.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 1 | Page 3 of 6

Pause and Choose: Separate Mood from Tone

A calm speaker calls a storm “a patient visitor tapping at every window,” while the house shakes. Which interpretation distinguishes speaker attitude from reader experience?

A. “The tone and mood are both calm because the speaker uses the word ‘patient.’”
Not the best choice. The speaker’s controlled description may sound calm, but the shaking house complicates the atmosphere readers experience.
B. “The speaker’s tone is composed, but the patient tapping and shaking house create an uneasy mood because calm language makes the threat feel persistent.”
✓ Correct—the response identifies two related but distinct effects. It connects tone to the speaker’s phrasing and mood to the reader’s experience of the storm’s steady pressure.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Lesson: Designing Mood with Figurative Language

Five-Step Analysis

  1. Read literally: state what is physically happening.
  2. Mark the device: name the exact comparison, personification, image, symbol, or sound pattern.
  3. Unpack associations: list what the key words suggest beyond denotation.
  4. Name a precise mood: choose a defensible word such as foreboding, hushed, buoyant, or wistful—not simply good or bad.
  5. Prove the effect: connect quoted detail → device → association → mood. Check whether another detail complicates the mood.

Visual Mood Map

Exact wordsDevice / senseAssociationReader effect
“windows swallowed the sun”personification, sightlight consumedforeboding confinement

Pause and Choose: Trace Figurative Language to Mood

Read: “The windows swallowed the last strip of sun.” Which analysis completes the full evidence chain?

A. “The personification creates a dark mood because the sentence mentions sunset.”
Not the best choice. “Dark” is vague, and the answer skips the association created by “swallowed.” Merely naming sunset does not explain the device’s effect.
B. “Giving the windows the action ‘swallowed’ makes the light seem consumed, creating a foreboding mood of enclosure or approaching loss.”
✓ Correct—the reasoning connects every link. It quotes the exact word, names personification, unpacks the association of consumption, and identifies a precise reader effect.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Learning Routes

  • Visual: color-code sensory details and mood shifts.
  • Auditory: read aloud and mark where sound or rhythm changes feeling.
  • Hands-on: replace one key word with three alternatives and compare the mood.

Mood Is Not Tone

Mood belongs to the reader’s experience; tone describes the speaker’s attitude. A calm speaker can describe a threatening setting, producing an uneasy mood. Always identify whose feeling you are naming.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 1 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Mood Models

Example 1 — Simile and Sound

Lines: “Rain tapped like careful fingers / along the locked glass.”
Literal: Rain strikes a window.
Device: Simile compares rain to deliberate fingers; repeated soft sounds slow the line.
Association: “Careful” suggests secrecy and restraint; “locked” adds separation.
Mood: Hushed uneasiness.
Evidence chain: The gentle tapping seems controlled rather than random, making the quiet feel watchful.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which analysis most clearly connects the simile to the mood?

A. The rain is compared to fingers, so the line is descriptive and therefore creates a mood.
Weaker response. This identifies the device but does not explain how its precise language shapes the reader’s feeling.
B. Comparing the rain to “careful fingers” makes the tapping seem deliberate, while “locked glass” adds separation; together the details create a hushed, watchful uneasiness.
Stronger response. This response traces two pieces of evidence through association to a precise mood.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Personification and Connotation

Lines: “Morning elbowed through the curtains, / rude with gold.”
Literal: Bright sunlight enters.
Device: Morning is personified as pushing; “elbowed” and “rude” have intrusive connotations.
Mood: Irritated urgency, not peaceful warmth.
Revision test: Replacing “elbowed” with “drifted” changes the mood to calm, proving diction controls the effect.

Example 3 — Symbol and Mood Shift

Lines: “All winter the porch swing wore snow. / In March, one red mitten waited there.”
Literal: Snow covers a swing; a mitten appears.
Pattern: Empty swing suggests absence; the bright mitten becomes a symbol of return or remembered presence.
Shift: Desolation becomes cautious hope.
Nuance: “One” still implies incompleteness, so the hope is not certainty.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: Read “The porch light blinked like a tired eye.” Name the device and explain one mood it could create without inventing a plot.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: The simile compares the light to a tired eye. “Blinked” and “tired” may create a weary or uneasy mood because the light seems weak and watchful, though the line does not establish why.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 1 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Figurative Language and Mood

Purpose

Use figurative language deliberately to establish and sustain a specific mood.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Make deliberate choices that demonstrate the lesson skill.

Source for Your Work

The hallway swallowed every footstep. / Lockers stood like patient witnesses / while the last bell shivered through the glass.

1. Plan Before You Draft

Poetic DecisionYour Plan
Speaker, situation, and intended effectState each precisely.
Image or language patternList two connected possibilities.
Turn or developmentDescribe what changes and why.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger poetic craft? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. The hallway was scary and empty, and the student felt nervous.
B. The hallway swallowed every footstep while the last bell shivered through the glass.

3. Apply the Lesson

Write a 12–16 line poem or a 250–300 word lyrical scene that creates one clear mood. Use at least three purposeful figures of speech and concrete sensory details.

4. Revise with Purpose

Underline one comparison that feels predictable. Replace it with a fresher image and explain how the revision strengthens the mood.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your original writing applies the lesson skill and uses the supplied source or model.
  • Your explanation identifies a specific craft choice and its effect.
  • Your revision improves meaning or craft, not only spelling.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Figurative Language and Mood

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original writing, and explain your craft decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: Platform at Dawn

The train station yawns beneath a bruised-blue sky. A single lamp keeps watch while rain stitches silver lines across the tracks. My suitcase waits beside me like a question I cannot answer.

Figurative language creates meaning beyond literal wording. Mood is the emotional atmosphere a reader experiences.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Identify two examples of figurative language. Explain what each comparison or image suggests beyond its literal meaning.
  2. What mood does the passage create? Cite two words or phrases and explain how their connotations build that mood.

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant word, line, or image, and explain how it proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which response analyzes how figurative language creates mood rather than merely summarizing details?

A. The station is quiet and it is raining. The speaker has a suitcase.
B. The personified station “yawns” while the lamp “keeps watch,” creating a lonely, uncertain mood as the speaker faces departure.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Write a 14–18 line original poem that creates one intentional mood.

  1. Opening image: Place the reader in a specific moment or setting.
  2. Development: Use at least three purposeful examples of figurative language, including two different techniques.
  3. Turn: Shift the speaker’s understanding, emotion, or focus.
  4. Close: End with an image that deepens the mood instead of explaining it.

After the poem, identify your three figurative choices and explain how each contributes to the mood.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the reader should experience, how each movement will build that effect, and which words and images will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Replace one predictable comparison with a fresher image. Explain how the new wording changes or sharpens the mood.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise the organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the writing becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The writing follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
